title: Solve a system by choosing better directions

blocks.text: Following the residual direction alone can repeatedly undo progress made along an earlier direction. Conjugate gradient constructs directions that are orthogonal in the A-defined inner product. Each new direction explores information that previous directions have not already resolved. This is particularly valuable when A is large and sparse, because matrix-vector products can be cheaper than a factorization.

## Task: Implement the Conjugate Gradient Method for Solving Linear Systems

Your task is to implement the Conjugate Gradient (CG) method, an efficient iterative algorithm for solving large, sparse, symmetric, positive-definite linear systems. Given a matrix `A` and a vector `b`, the algorithm will solve for `x` in the system \( Ax = b \).

Write a function `conjugate_gradient(A, b, n, x0=None, tol=1e-8)` that performs the Conjugate Gradient method as follows:

- `A`: A symmetric, positive-definite matrix representing the linear system.
- `b`: The vector on the right side of the equation.
- `n`: Maximum number of iterations.
- `x0`: Initial guess for the solution vector.
- `tol`: Tolerance for stopping criteria.

The function should return the solution vector `x`.

A linear system Ax=b asks for a vector whose matrix product equals a target. The residual b−Ax measures the mismatch. A symmetric positive-definite matrix defines a bowl-shaped quadratic with one minimizer; this is the setting required by conjugate gradient.

The animation starts from zero and shows a two-dimensional example. A two-dimensional positive-definite system can be solved in at most two exact-arithmetic CG iterations, but finite precision and larger systems require tolerance-based stopping. Watch the residual norm alongside the path: movement in the plot is useful only if the equation mismatch decreases toward zero.

blocks.text: Connect the picture to the mathematics

blocks.caption: r is the residual, p is the search direction, and alpha is the step length. The matrix A defines the geometry in which search directions are conjugate.

blocks.text: The step length uses the current residual norm squared divided by pᵀAp. Positive definiteness makes the denominator positive for a nonzero direction. After updating x, the residual is updated without solving a new system. The next direction combines the new residual with a scaled previous direction. Changing the matrix changes the bowl geometry and therefore the path.

The preserved workbook solution accepts x0 in its signature but initializes x to zero unconditionally. This lesson does not silently repair that discrepancy; the demonstrated cases use a zero start. It also does not precheck an initially zero residual before its first division. When adapting this code, address those edge cases explicitly. The numerical examples here are checked against np.linalg.solve and use floating-point inputs to avoid integer truncation.
